p.x:
My favourite book is about a brave princess and a dragon. The title is 'The Girl Who Flew'. The cover is blue, with a picture of the princess on the dragon's back.
In the story, the princess lives in a castle, but she thinks her life is boring. One day, she finds a small dragon in the garden. The dragon is hurt, so she helps it. Soon, they become best friends, and the dragon teaches her to fly!
The book has 120 pages, but I read it in two days because it was so interesting. My teacher says reading is good for my English. Now I read every night before bed.

Last Saturday, I went to the city library with my friend Nam. It's much bigger than the bookshop near my house. We asked the librarian where we could find mystery books. "Second floor," she said, "next to the fairy tales."
Nam loves romance stories, but I prefer books with magic and adventure. I borrowed a book about a boy who discovers he is a wizard. I read the first chapter in the library, and it was great. The villain is very scary!
The library also has e-books. You can download them to your phone for free with your library card. Nam says she prefers real books because she likes turning the pages. I don't mind. For me, the most important thing is a good ending.

In an age of short videos and endless notifications, some people argue that reading novels is a luxury. Why spend hours on fiction when non-fiction, such as a biography or a science book, can teach us facts? Researchers, however, have found that reading fiction offers benefits that are not easily replaced.
One of the most interesting findings concerns empathy. When we follow a protagonist through difficult decisions, especially when the story is told by a first-person narrator, we practise seeing the world through someone else's eyes. Studies suggest that regular readers of literary fiction perform better on tests that measure the ability to understand other people's emotions.
Good fiction also trains attention. A thriller with a cliffhanger at the end of every chapter may be a page-turner, but even slower novels, with their rich setting and careful prose, ask us to concentrate for long periods. Readers learn to notice details, to interpret metaphor and symbolism, and to wait patiently for a twist that changes everything.
The publishing industry has changed enormously. A writer who once had to send a manuscript to dozens of publishers can now self-publish an e-book online, and some of these have become international bestsellers. Audiobooks, too, have attracted millions of new 'readers'. Whatever the format, stories remain essential. Long before paperbacks or even writing existed, humans told myths around the fire. Fantasy and science fiction, perhaps, are simply the modern versions of those ancient stories, and an autobiography is just a story we tell about ourselves.
